summary: For ages 8–9, pupils construct a claim–evidence–reasoning argument that living in a group raises an individual animal's chance of surviving and reproducing. The core is comparing the same animal alone vs in a group so the survival benefit is a concrete, pointable difference across three benefit families: protection (shared vigilance, dilution, mobbing), finding/catching food (cooperative hunting such as wolf packs, and information sharing such as bees' waggle dance), and raising young / division of labour (colony castes). Pupils also weigh costs (competition, disease) so they argue a net benefit rather than assume grouping is always best, and they frame the benefit at the level of the individual rather than as deliberate altruism 'for the good of the species'. A comparison simulation makes the mechanism visible; a questioning naturalist dialogue, an annotated scene, and a knowledge check support different parts of the learning.
misconceptions: Thinking animals group because they 'like company' or 'are friends', rather than for survival advantages.
Believing bigger groups are always safer, ignoring costs like competition for food and faster disease spread.
Assuming grouping helps the group as a whole in a way disconnected from each individual's own survival/reproduction.
Treating 'construct an argument' as 'describe the animal', omitting evidence and reasoning.

activities.title: Alone vs together: a savanna, pack and colony survival comparison
steps: Run a single gazelle on the savanna: it can graze OR lift its head to scan for lions, but not both (a simplified model of the vigilance trade-off), so it feeds little and is repeatedly ambushed; watch its survival meter sink.

Drop the gazelle into a herd and watch the mechanism work: with many animals, some keep their heads up while others feed, a lion is spotted while still far off, and each animal's feeding AND survival meters climb.
Switch to a wolf scenario: watch one lone wolf tire and lose an elk, then watch a coordinated pack succeed in bringing it down.
Switch to an ant colony where division of labour (foragers, guards, carers) out-survives a single lone forager.
Use a 'build your argument' capture that logs the specific evidence you observed (who spotted the predator, who ate, who succeeded) to reuse in a written or spoken argument.
activities.insight: The survival advantage of grouping emerges from a mechanism you can see — shared vigilance and cooperation — so it can be argued from observed evidence rather than simply asserted.

activities.title: Naturalist debrief: defend your claim with evidence
steps: State a survival claim about the animal you observed in the sim (e.g. 'living in a herd keeps a gazelle safer').
Respond to an in-role naturalist who accepts the claim only when backed by a specific mechanism and example: 'You say the herd is safer — what's your evidence?'
Answer a counter-challenge that surfaces costs: 'But doesn't a big herd attract more predators, or spread disease faster?' and refine your argument to a net benefit.
Transfer the structure to a second group-living animal (e.g. a zebra herd, an ant colony, or a wolf pack) and argue a different benefit family.

Plan evidence: explain how you could actually gather evidence that animals in groups survive better than lone ones (e.g. compare how often a lone animal versus one in a group is caught, or how much each eats).
activities.insight: A scientific argument is a claim supported by specific evidence and reasoning about a mechanism, and it holds up even when costs are raised — it is not just a description of the animal, and the benefit is something each individual gains, not a planned act of kindness.

activities.title: Annotated group scene: spot the survival benefit
steps: Explore an annotated scene of a herd, a hunting pack and a colony.

Tap callouts to reveal the survival benefit each feature provides: a sentinel meerkat with its head up (protection), a pack formation encircling prey and bees sharing a food location with a waggle dance (finding/catching food), and ant castes queen, workers, guards (raising young / division of labour).
Name which benefit family each callout belongs to: protection, food, or raising young / division of labour.
activities.insight: Each of the three benefit families has concrete, recognisable mechanisms in real species that can later be cited as evidence.

activities.title: Knowledge check: the three benefit families
steps: Answer a question such as 'How does a herd protect an individual?' choosing the mechanism (many eyes spot the predator / any one animal is less likely to be caught) rather than a feelings-based answer.
Match each animal to the survival benefit it gains (wolves → cooperative hunting; ants → division of labour; gazelles → shared vigilance; fish schools → dilution/confusion of the predator).
activities.insight: Recall of the three benefit families and their species anchors the evidence a learner needs before building an argument.

activities.title: Predict-Observe-Explain: is a cluster safer than a lone runner?
steps: Before playing, predict whether a lone runner or a runner inside a tight cluster of ten is more likely to be tagged in a single lunge by a 'predator', and say WHY.

Run the game, where the tagger can grab at most one runner per lunge (a chosen game rule to model dilution). If the tagger lunges at the cluster about as often as at the lone runner, any one individual in the cluster should be caught less often than the lone runner; count tags to check.

Explain the result, connecting it to dilution (any one animal is less likely to be the one caught in each attack); shared vigilance would need runners who can watch for the tagger, which this game does not model.
activities.insight: In each attack, being in a group lowers any single individual's chance of being the one caught. A crowd may be easier for predators to notice, but each member's risk per attack is shared out. This is a measurable survival effect for the individual, not a matter of the animals' feelings.

checkQuestion: Say: 'Zebras live in big herds. Does living in a herd actually help a zebra survive — or do they just like being together? Give me your reason, and tell me HOW being in a herd could help a zebra when a lion attacks.'
checkAnswer: Living in a herd gives concrete survival advantages: many eyes spot the lion sooner (vigilance); any one zebra is less likely to be the one caught (safety in numbers / dilution); the herd can confuse the predator and defend its young. It is not simply that they 'like company' — the grouping produces measurable survival benefits that can be supported with evidence.
